papers.title: Desired Fertility, Realized Fertility and the Effects of China’s Universal Two-Child Policy
Addressing Population Ageing in China: Public Policy and Institutional Innovations
papers.venue: Cambridge University Press Elements Series in Chinese Economy and Governance (book)
papers.abstract: China is entering a new demographic era marked by sustained population decline and rapid population ageing. Drawing on Chinese government statistics, international datasets, and recent academic evidence, this Element documents the speed and uneven geography of China’s transition, diagnoses its economic and social consequences, and proposes a portfolio of policy and institutional innovations. After an introductory section, Section 2 establishes the facts and drivers: fertility has fallen to among the world’s lowest levels while life expectancy has risen sharply, pushing the share of older adults upward and compressing the working-age population, with especially fast ageing in many rural and interior regions. Section 3 traces the downstream impact of this phenomenon on the social insurance systems and the real economy. It highlights mounting pressure on pay-as-you-go pensions, rising health and long-term care needs amid weakening family-based support, and emerging risks for labor supply, productivity, savings, and social cohesion—particularly as caregiving burdens fall disproportionately on women. Section 4 develops China-focused but internationally relevant innovations to “grow old without growing poor:” expanding safe home-equity release (including redesigned reverse mortgages), extending productive working lives through retirement-age reform paired with job redesign and reskilling, scaling long-term care insurance and service capacity, and strengthening community-based solutions such as time banking and senior co-housing. The Element also reviews evidence on pro-family policies, emphasizing childcare provision and work–family compatibility instead of one-off cash incentives. China’s vast size and heterogeneity create exceptional scope for experimentation and policy learning, offering lessons for other countries confronting similar ageing challenges. This Element complements existing policy options laid out by the Chinese government and other organizations such as the World Bank.
